mcqs.question: Two author-stylesheet rules with equal specificity target the same property on the same element. Which one wins?
options: Neither — the browser falls back to the user-agent default
Whichever rule appears later in source order
Whichever rule has more total selectors written, regardless of type
Whichever rule was defined in an external stylesheet rather than an inline style tag
mcqs.explanation: Source order is the cascade's last tiebreaker, used only once origin/importance and specificity are both tied — the later rule wins. Total selector count doesn't matter once specificity is already established as equal, and a user-agent fallback would only apply if there were no author rule at all.

mcqs.question: What is the specificity tuple of the selector `.card .title.large`?
options: (0, 3, 0) — three class selectors, no ID, no elements
(0, 0, 2) — treated as two element-level selectors
(1, 2, 0) — the compound selector counts as an implicit ID
(0, 2, 1) — one of the classes is miscounted as an element
mcqs.explanation: There are three class selectors (.card, .title, .large) and neither an ID nor an element/type selector, so the tuple is (0, 3, 0). Compound selectors don't create implicit IDs, and classes are never counted in the element position.

mcqs.question: Selector A is `.nav .item .link .icon` (0,4,0) and selector B is `#app span` (1,0,1). Which wins, and why?
options: A wins, because it has more total selector tokens
It's a tie, resolved by source order, because both selectors target similar elements
A wins, because classes are weighted higher than IDs in modern CSS
B wins, because the tuple comparison is positional — a nonzero ID count in the first position beats any number of classes in the second
mcqs.explanation: Specificity tuples compare left to right, position by position — B's single ID gives it a nonzero value in the very first slot, which A's zero can never overcome regardless of how many classes A stacks in the second slot. IDs are not weighted lower than classes, and this isn't a tie of any kind.

mcqs.question: A team has three layers of `!important` stacked on the same property across different stylesheets, each added to override the previous one. What does this situation actually indicate?
options: That specificity is being calculated incorrectly by the browser
That the CSS is fine, since !important always resolves conflicts safely
That earlier overrides used !important as a quick fix, and each new override needed the same escape hatch to win, escalating instead of fixing the underlying specificity issue
That the browser will pick the first !important declaration it parses and ignore the rest
mcqs.explanation: !important stacking is a classic escalation pattern — once one override reaches for it, any later override needs the same tool to win, and normal specificity reasoning stops applying. Among multiple !important declarations the normal specificity/source-order rules still apply at that elevated tier, so it isn't simply "first one wins," and nothing here indicates a browser calculation bug.

mcqs.question: With `@layer base, components;` declared, a rule in the `components` layer uses a plain class selector while a rule in `base` uses `#app .thing` with a much higher specificity. Which one applies?
options: The base rule, since layers only affect source order, not which one wins
Whichever rule has !important applied, regardless of layer
The components rule, because layer order is checked before specificity, and components was declared later
The base rule, because higher specificity always wins first regardless of layers
mcqs.explanation: Cascade layers are a tiebreaker that sits above specificity entirely — a later-declared layer beats an earlier one no matter how specific the earlier layer's selector is. Specificity is only compared within the same layer, so base's higher specificity never even enters the comparison here.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't setting `margin: 20px` on a parent element also apply that margin to its children by default?
options: margin is a non-inheriting property by default, unlike typography properties such as color and font-size
Margin only inherits when box-sizing is set to border-box
Inheritance was disabled entirely for any property introduced after CSS2
Children always override inherited margin with a default of 0 regardless of the property's inheritance rules
mcqs.explanation: Box-model properties like margin, padding, and width don't inherit by default because a child sharing its parent's exact spacing would rarely make layout sense — unlike typography properties, which are designed to cascade down naturally. Inheritance behavior is per-property by specification, not tied to box-sizing or a CSS-version cutoff.
